Ná déanaimid dearúd: 'Ní neart go cur le chéile'.

discussion.speaker: Sara MATTHIEU
discussion.text:
Madam President, last week I read about a woman in Paris. She was 80 years old. She lived on the top floor of an apartment. There was no cooling. There was just some fans. It was 47 degrees out there in her apartment, and she died there – alone.

And many others did this June. In France, deaths at home rose by 91 %. In Belgium, we lost 1 222 people in only 12 days during the heatwave.

And in the same week, the cooling systems in the data centres never stopped running for a second, because the industry standard says that they can never get warmer than 27 degrees. How can we have cooling rules for machines and not for people?

I urge the Irish Presidency to put this high on the agenda. We must regulate data centres, take concrete action against heatwaves, and we must protect people. Because computers don't pay taxes. They don't die alone in an attic. People do. So let's protect the people first.

discussion.speaker: Luke Ming FLANAGAN
discussion.text:
A Uachtaráin, fáilte romhat, a Mhichíl. Fáilte romhat, a Thomáis.

Madam President, when I got elected to the European Parliament, I got elected as a sceptic. I got elected because I was told by the Irish Government continuously when they weren't happy with the EU enforcing rules, that they were made to do it. I have discovered otherwise.

And since I got elected here, I have to say I believe the common agricultural policy is the most important policy of the European Union. In my county alone, a county of 80 000 people, EUR 1 billion in CAP payments has come to Roscommon since I was elected in 2014. Over the same period, in the future, if we stick with current budgetary proposals on the MFF, we would see a reduction in payments of EUR 200 million just to Roscommon, excluding inflation.

All the more reason then that we get this right when deciding who gets this money. In the Commission proposal, the text refers to those most in need. To me, the most in need are those that farm marginal lands on smallholdings and those on designated lands. We also need to respect those pluriactive farmers who, while not making a full-time living out of farming, are nonetheless contributing in a significant way to food sovereignty and the provision of public goods – the latter of which has never been properly remunerated for.

The proposals on fisheries are even worse: from 6 billion to 2 billion. As with agri funding, this means it has now been never more important that small-scale, low impact fishers are given this money. The money must be provided in a way that fishers can actually access it. As things stands, that is not the case.

Finally, in relation to defective concrete, when are you going to get your act together? Infringement proceedings remain open. They do so in spite of the fact that thousands of people's lives have been blighted by crumbling houses. The danger of this issue repeating itself remains very real. The European Parliament has backed this. You now need to do something about it. People deserve dignity. They don't have it.

discussion.speaker: Petr BYSTRON
discussion.text:
Liebe Frau Präsidentin, Micheál Martin, Maroš Šefčovič, liebe Kolleginnen und Kollegen! Drei Punkte hat der Kollege hier hervorgehoben: wirtschaftliche Prosperität, Werte und Sicherheit. Wirtschaftliche Prosperität hat die EU selbst zerstört durch die unsinnigen Embargos gegen Russland. Unsere Unternehmen haben jetzt die teuersten Energiepreise, sind nicht mehr konkurrenzfähig auf den Weltmärkten, verlassen die Europäische Union oder gehen pleite. Gleichzeitig zahlt die Europäische Union an die Ukraine – 300 Mrd. Euro waren das in dem ganzen Zeitraum seit Anfang des Krieges.

Und wie viel geht in die Forschung, zur Förderung der Wirtschaft und der Prosperität? Der Forschungs- und Innovationsfonds bekommt 90 Milliarden, lediglich 90 Milliarden im gleichen Zeitraum, und mickrige 10 Milliarden davon sind für Start-ups. Wir müssen die Embargos beenden und die Wirtschaft und Innovation stärken.

Werte? Über welche Werte reden Sie? Gleich wird hier abgestimmt über das Verbot der EU-Partei, der stärksten Partei in Deutschland, auf Antrag der Kommunisten, Sozialisten und der Grünen: Das sind die wahren Feinde der Demokratie; hier werden demokratische Werte, europäische Werte mit Füßen getreten.

Und Sicherheit? Sicherheit in der EU? Ich bin gespannt. Erklären Sie das den zwei kleinen Mädchen und der Ehefrau von dem schwedischen Polizisten Christian Zedig, der neulich umgebracht wurde. Sie haben in der EU die Sicherheit der EU-Bürger durch die Massenmigration zerstört. Und nur wir, nur wir durch die Remigration, wir liefern bereits aus der Opposition, und wir beschützen die Bürger Europas.

translation.englishText:
Dear Madam President, Micheál Martin, Maroš Šefčovič, dear colleagues! The colleague highlighted three points here: economic prosperity, values ​​and security. The EU itself has destroyed economic prosperity through the senseless embargoes against Russia. Our companies now have the most expensive energy prices, are no longer competitive on world markets, are leaving the European Union or are going bankrupt. At the same time, the European Union is paying Ukraine 300 billion euros in the entire period since the beginning of the war.

And how much goes into research to promote the economy and prosperity? The research and innovation fund gets 90 billion, just 90 billion in the same period, and a measly 10 billion of that is for start-ups. We must end the embargoes and strengthen the economy and innovation.

Values? What values ​​are you talking about? A vote is about to take place here to ban the EU party, the strongest party in Germany, at the request of the communists, socialists and the Greens: These are the real enemies of democracy; Democratic values ​​and European values ​​are being trampled on here.

And security? Security in the EU? I am excited. Explain this to the two little girls and the wife of the Swedish policeman Christian Zedig, who was recently killed. They have destroyed the security of EU citizens in the EU through mass migration. And only we, only we through remigration, we are already delivering from the opposition, and we are protecting the citizens of Europe.

discussion.speaker: Fernand KARTHEISER
discussion.text:
Madam President, Taoiseach, Ireland's Presidency must not be a presidency like all the others. Many Europeans hope Ireland will build on its own proud history and independent character, rather than obediently fulfil the Commission's agenda.

Ireland is a neutral country and should oppose the EU's transformation into a European NATO. Instead of supporting the escalation and prolongation of conflicts, it should use its presidency to guide Europe towards diplomacy and a negotiated settlement with our Russian neighbours.

Ireland is a proudly Catholic country. It should oppose generalised same‑sex parental recognition and surrogacy in the EU. Ireland should stand firm in defending our children's rights against those who merchandise them, as well as their biological mothers.

The Irish are freedom‑loving people. Please fight now to abolish EU censorship, the Democracy Shield and regulated access to social media. I wish the Irish Presidency courage and success for its 8th Council presidency.

discussion.speaker: Siegfried MUREŞAN
discussion.text:
Madam President, Prime Minister, Taoiseach, colleagues, welcome to the European Parliament.

Look, a very vast majority of the Members of the European Parliament agree that the priorities of the Union for the upcoming months are, firstly, defending European values, protecting our democracy, our freedoms. Secondly, investing more in our security, in our defence, protecting citizens. And thirdly, strengthening the economy, making it more competitive, ready for the digital age and for artificial intelligence.

Prime Minister, the programme of the Irish Presidency that you are putting forward today identifies these priorities also as the priorities of the Irish Presidency. This is correct. We thank you for this. In addition to this, we also very much welcome your focus on enlargement. Supporting and strengthening our neighbouring countries, which are also EU candidate countries is good for the candidate countries, but it is good for the Union as well. The stronger, the more stable the candidate countries are, the better also for the security of the 27 Member States. So, full support also for your ambitious merit‑based enlargement agenda.

If we want Europe to do more to protect its citizens, to become more competitive, we have to equip it with the right tools. One of the tools is the budget of the European Union. We as a Parliament, at the end of April, have adopted our common position on the EU budget for the next seven years, identifying security and competitiveness as the new priorities of the budget, but not neglecting what has proven its viability in time: protecting fisheries, protecting farmers, protecting our regions. We want a future‑oriented, modern cohesion policy.

It is clear that when it comes to the budget, we can't do more with less. This is why we stand for an ambitious budget. Please make sure that, as we have a Parliament's position, there will be a Council position by the end of the year, based also on the transparent introduction of our own sources of revenue of the European Union.

discussion.speaker: Carla TAVARES
discussion.text:
Senhora Presidente, Senhor Comissário, começo naturalmente por saudar a Presidência irlandesa e estou certa de que a cooperação com este Parlamento será estreita e profícua.

Sabemos também que uma das prioridades é o orçamento de longo prazo da União e sabemos bem, também, de um compromisso de um trabalho intenso e ambicioso com todos os líderes da União Europeia para que seja possível ter um acordo até ao final de 2026.

Como a Senhora Presidente sabe, para o Parlamento Europeu, para nós, é absolutamente claro que é preciso que esse acordo exista até ao final do ano.

Mas não é possível trabalhar no QFP olhando só para o lado da despesa. É importante olharmos também para a ambição orçamental e é preciso olhar para a receita. Falo, obviamente, dos novos recursos próprios que tornem o orçamento europeu mais justo, mais robusto e menos dependente das contribuições nacionais.

Não se pode fazer mais com menos e este Parlamento apoia a abordagem da Comissão de um cabaz para obter um acordo sobre novos recursos próprios.

Precisamos de uma União Europeia mais segura, competitiva e coesa e de um orçamento à altura dessa ambição. Novas prioridades requerem maior investimento. Uma Europa mais forte exige um orçamento também mais forte.

translation.englishText:
Madam President, Commissioner, I naturally begin by welcoming the Irish Presidency and I am sure that cooperation with this Parliament will be close and fruitful.

We also know that one of the priorities is the Union's long-term budget and we are also well aware of a commitment to intense and ambitious work with all European Union leaders so that it is possible to have an agreement by the end of 2026.

As Madam President knows, for the European Parliament, for us, it is absolutely clear that this agreement needs to exist by the end of the year.

But it is not possible to work on the MFF looking only at the expenditure side. It is important that we also look at the budgetary ambition and we need to look at revenue. I am obviously talking about new own resources that make the European budget fairer, more robust and less dependent on national contributions.

More cannot be done with less and this Parliament supports the Commission's basket approach to reaching agreement on new own resources.

We need a safer, more competitive and cohesive European Union and a budget that matches this ambition. New priorities require greater investment. A stronger Europe also requires a stronger budget.

discussion.speaker: Marieke EHLERS
discussion.text:
Madam President, Prime Minister, Commissioner, Europeans are asking simple but existential questions. How do we pay for food, electricity and rent? Will we still have a job tomorrow? And why are our streets no longer safe for our women and children? These are the concerns of ordinary citizens.

Yet in your chapter on security, I find little to nothing about criminal migrants or returning those with no right to stay. Instead, I read about 'security in all dimensions' and something called climate security. Interesting concepts, perhaps, but not the priorities citizens expect.

Europe does not need better migration management. It needs control of its borders. The priority should be rapid returns, not more legal migration pathways.

And on the next multiannual budget, taxpayers expect discipline and value for money. Instead, the Irish Presidency advocates a larger EU budget, higher national contributions and more common borrowing. But the answer to every challenge cannot be to throw more money at it.

And when it comes to the staggering energy prices, your programme mentions 'affordable energy' only three times. The word 'gender', on the other hand, appears 14 times.

Europe does not need more migration, more debt and more ideology. It needs realism, regulatory prudence and sound fiscal policy.

discussion.speaker: Assita KANKO
discussion.text:
Madam President, in all what you said, presidency, I haven't heard much about antisemitism, yet a big issue in Europe. As you know, we still need to protect Jewish schools and institutions in many European cities, and that is a fact.

You speak of the importance of our European way of life and I totally welcome that. I must say what it means today, though. You need to give faith to European people again, faith in justice, faith in equality, faith in what the soul of Europe is. To me, it means that values are not à la carte.

It means we all have access to the same justice, that no woman is subject to marital captivity or reduced to parallel justice systems. We need a Europe that says no to radical Islam and designate the Muslim Brotherhood as a terror organisation. We need a Europe that protects its children against sexual abuse online. For six years, we have been talking but never delivered regarding the regulation. Some of the children abused today were even not born.

Today, I will vote for the urgent procedure, but we need you to deliver ...

(The President cut off the speaker)

discussion.speaker: Michael MCNAMARA
discussion.text:
A Uachtaráin, is éacht pearsanta duit an lá seo, a Thaoisigh. Guím gach ádh ort agus go n-éirí leat.

The success of the Irish Presidency will be built on long hours by countless Irish civil servants far from today's limelight and that of recent days, and I think we should remember their work and wish them success as well in their important tasks.

As we assume leadership of the EU budget, we must lead by example. Try to do more with less, not less with more. We need to invest in our beleaguered defence forces, but that does not mean abandoning the proud role of neutral, non-aligned states, and our place among them.

Instead, we're spending EUR 293 million on this presidency. It's far too much, Taoiseach. Pull back on it, it's not necessary. Included in that is EUR 135 000 for wool scarves to be of uniquely Irish artistic character, but not necessarily Irish wool. It's 30 degrees outside, Taoiseach. When it does cool down, everybody around here is well capable of buying their own scarves.

When it does cool down, everybody around here is well capable of buying their own scarves.

discussion.speaker: Thomas WAITZ
discussion.text:
Mr President, Taoiseach, Commissioner, first of all, thank you for your preparation already towards this presidency. I see you are very active already in preparing and your people are around also talking to many of us.

I have three wishes to you to send in your direction. Ireland is hosting family farming and Ireland is hosting relatively small and medium-sized farming. We are negotiating the common agricultural policy. I count on you that you help us, that we support real farmers, and we don't dilute a European taxpayers' money to big investment funds or super-rich investors across the European Union. And we can really safeguard so that the farmers that work hard on their land and that also work in a climate, animal welfare and environmentally friendly way have access to the funds.

In this combination, also please make sure that this renationalisation of European money is not leading to a fragmentation and a distortion of markets – that we still keep the 'common' in our policy, whether it may be the common agricultural policy or others.

And thank you for standing up for enlargement and for this cooperation.

discussion.speaker: Jeroen LENAERS
discussion.text:
Madam President, dear colleagues, welcome Taoiseach, as my Member State has been paired with County Mayo during your presidency, I have to start by congratulating Mayo for reaching the semi‑finals at the expense of your very own Cork – Mayo for Sam! On a more serious note, the Irish Presidency has chosen three clear priorities: competitiveness, values and security, joined together under the motto 'Strength with unity', and that is both timely and appropriate.

On competitiveness: Europe must become more productive and competitive. We must continue cutting unnecessary bureaucracy and creating the conditions for businesses to invest, innovate and grow. But that alone will not be enough. We must also strengthen our industry, deepen our internal market and realise true strategic autonomy.

On values: protecting our values also means protecting our children. They deserve to grow up in a safe online environment protected from exploitation and harmful content, and I count on the Irish Presidency to make online child safety a central priority throughout its term, as it has done successfully at home.

Finally, security: Europe must continue to stand with Ukraine, but every Member State must contribute in a more fair share if Europe wants to remain credible.

Colleagues, there are many challenges, but they all require the same response: a Europe that acts together with determination. That is how we turn 'Strength with unity' from a motto into a lasting legacy.

discussion.speaker: Jean-Marc GERMAIN
discussion.text:
Madame la Présidente, Monsieur le Premier ministre, au moment où il vous revient de présider les négociations sur le budget pluriannuel, nous voulons vous adresser un message clair: on ne construit pas la compétitivité en sacrifiant la solidarité ou en léguant une planète invivable à nos enfants. Car, comme le dit le proverbe irlandais: «C’est en nous abritant les uns les autres que nous vivons.» Aussi, tant que le Conseil ne renoncera pas à liquider le Fonds européen ou à rogner les Fonds de cohésion pour financer le Fonds de compétitivité, il n’y aura pas de consentement du Parlement européen.

L’autre clash annoncé, c’est sur l’écologie. Je vois bien les tentations de tuer le principe consistant à «ne pas causer de préjudice important» à coups de dérogations, qui permettraient aux bénéficiaires de l’argent européen de s’asseoir sur les dégâts collatéraux qu’ils font subir à la nation. Mais j’ose espérer que, après l’épisode terrible de canicule que nous venons de vivre, votre présidence portera haut cette idée que, si l’union fait la force, l’unité se forge dans la justice sociale et dans la responsabilité environnementale.

translation.englishText:
Madam President, Mr Prime Minister, at a time when it is up to you to chair the negotiations on the multiannual budget, we want to send you a clear message: we do not build competitiveness by sacrificing solidarity or by bequeathing an unlivable planet to our children. Because, as the Irish proverb says: “It is by sheltering each other that we live.” Also, as long as the Council does not give up liquidating the European Fund or cutting back the Cohesion Funds to finance the Competitiveness Fund, there will be no consent from the European Parliament.

The other clash announced is over ecology. I can clearly see the temptations to kill the principle of “not causing significant harm” with derogations, which would allow the beneficiaries of European money to sit on the collateral damage they inflict on the nation. But I dare to hope that, after the terrible heatwave episode that we have just experienced, your presidency will uphold this idea that, if there is strength in unity, unity is forged in social justice and environmental responsibility.

discussion.speaker: Valérie DELOGE
discussion.text:
Madame la Présidente, chers collègues, aujourd’hui, nos agriculteurs n’étouffent pas sous le manque de promesses, ils étouffent sous leur accumulation. L’Union européenne est devenue une usine à contraintes. Le programme de la présidence irlandaise affiche de beaux objectifs: compétitivité, sécurité alimentaire, simplification. Dans les faits, elle recycle des débats interminables qui encombrent et étouffent encore un peu plus ceux qui produisent.

Nos agriculteurs et nos producteurs n’ont pas besoin de longs discours, ils ont besoin de revenus dignes et d’une vision à long terme. Pourtant, ils subissent une triple peine: des importations qui ne respectent pas nos standards, des coûts et des règles qui changent sans cesse et une bureaucratie qui est devenue hors de contrôle. On les enferme dans toujours plus de pacte vert, de De la ferme à la table, ou de baisse de la PAC, et d’écologie punitive.

Comment prétendre prioriser l’agriculture en réduisant et en désacralisant l’enveloppe de la PAC? Prenons l’élevage: ce n’est pas un problème à corriger, c’est une richesse à défendre, c’est un pilier de notre souveraineté.

Vous nous parlez d’autonomie, de facilité et de nouvelle agriculture sans jamais rencontrer, sans écouter et sans comprendre ce que vivent les agriculteurs. Nous attendons donc, pleins d’espoir, que cette nouvelle présidence entende les agriculteurs et défende une PAC forte, autonome, au service de la production et de ses producteurs.

translation.englishText:
Madam President, dear colleagues, today our farmers are not suffocating under the lack of promises, they are suffocating under their accumulation. The European Union has become a factory of constraints. The Irish presidency's program displays some fine objectives: competitiveness, food security, simplification. In fact, it recycles endless debates which further encumber and suffocate those who produce.

Our farmers and producers do not need long speeches, they need decent income and a long-term vision. Yet they suffer a triple penalty: imports that do not meet our standards, costs and rules that are constantly changing and a bureaucracy that has become out of control. We lock them into ever more green pact, from farm to table, or lowering of the CAP, and punitive ecology.

How can we claim to prioritize agriculture by reducing and desacralizing the CAP envelope? Let's take breeding: it is not a problem to correct, it is a wealth to defend, it is a pillar of our sovereignty.

You talk to us about autonomy, ease and new agriculture without ever meeting, without listening and without understanding what farmers experience. We therefore wait, full of hope, for this new presidency to listen to farmers and defend a strong, autonomous CAP, serving production and its producers.

discussion.speaker: Bogdan RZOŃCA
discussion.text:
Pani Przewodnicząca! Panie Premierze! Było dużo uprzejmości jak dotąd. A teraz parę szczegółów. Jeden z europejskich think tanków wyliczył właśnie, że w 2025 roku Unia Europejska straciła 90 miliardów euro, dlatego że jest ogromna ofensywa przemysłu chińskiego w Unii Europejskiej i upadają firmy. Mówimy dużo o Zielonym Ładzie, a ja chcę powiedzieć bardzo wyraźnie: najpierw energia powinna być tania dla przedsiębiorców, a później zielona.

Zwracam uwagę prezydencji irlandzkiej również na to, że historycznie Unia jest w tej chwili w największym długu. Jeszcze nigdy Unia Europejska nie była tak zadłużona, jak jest teraz. Mamy ogromny problem, czego świadkami są wszyscy obecni tu na tej sali, bo w Unii Europejskiej upadają firmy albo przenoszą swoją działalność do Indii, do Stanów Zjednoczonych. Ostatnio austriacka firma napisała wprost, gdy głosowaliśmy nad pomocą z funduszu globalizacji, że ucieka do Indii, bo nie wytrzymuje z cenami. Na takie rzeczy trzeba zwrócić uwagę. Życzę powodzenia.

translation.englishText:

One of the European think tanks has just calculated that in 2025 the European Union will lose EUR 90 billion because there is a huge offensive of the Chinese industry in the European Union and companies are going bankrupt. We talk a lot about the Green Deal, and I want to say it very clearly: first, energy should be cheap for entrepreneurs, and then green.

I also draw the attention of the Irish Presidency to the fact that, historically, the Union is currently in the greatest debt. The European Union has never been as indebted as it is now. We have a huge problem, as everyone present in this room is witnessing, because companies in the European Union are going bankrupt or moving their operations to India or to the United States. Recently, an Austrian company wrote directly, when we voted on aid from the globalization fund, that it was fleeing to India because it could not cope with the prices. You need to pay attention to such things. I wish you good luck.

discussion.speaker: Tomas TOBÉ
discussion.text:
Madam President, Commissioner, Taoiseach, the EPP Group strongly welcomes the Irish Presidency's focused on the security of Europe and its citizens. We have already strengthened Europe's external borders with the migration pact and new rules on returns of irregular migrants. Now, we must step up our fight against cross-border organised crime because, while we have taken back control of our external borders, criminal networks continue to abuse the freedom of movement within our Union.

Concretely, we count on the Irish Presidency to push for a stronger Europol and to make it into a truly operational police agency. Internal security must be reflected properly in the long‑term budget. Organised crime has never posed a greater threat to our citizens and our societies. We must do everything we can to crack down on it. The EPP is ready to work with the Irish Presidency. All the best...

(The President cut off the speaker)

discussion.speaker: Stefano CAVEDAGNA
discussion.text:
Signora Presidente, onorevoli colleghi, l'Europa ha due grandi priorità.

La prima: combattere tutte quelle follie green ed ecologiste che abbiamo visto nell'ultimo mandato, prima tra tutte l'ETS, quell'odiosa tassa ambientale che fa danni continuamente alle nostre imprese e ai nostri cittadini. Fermare il Green Deal: questo serve per una migliore competitività europea.

E l'altra, che non è seconda a questa prima priorità, è quella della sicurezza dei cittadini, la loro sicurezza che i cittadini europei pretendono di avere per le loro strade, nelle loro città, nelle loro nazioni.

E si combatte con due modalità. La prima è una lotta attiva al fondamentalismo islamico – rispetto al quale troppe persone qui in quest'Aula non stanno parlando, e lo stanno dimenticando – e l'altra è quella della lotta all'immigrazione clandestina: dobbiamo rimpatriare tutti gli immigrati illegali, perché, altrimenti, i problemi di sicurezza peggioreranno giorno dopo giorno, come hanno mostrato i recenti attacchi.

translation.englishText:
Madam President, ladies and gentlemen, Europe has two great priorities.

The first: fight all those green and ecological follies that we have seen in the last mandate, first of all the ETS, that hateful environmental tax that continually damages our businesses and our citizens. Stop the Green Deal: this is necessary for better European competitiveness.

And the other, which is not second to this first priority, is that of the safety of citizens, their safety that European citizens claim to have on their streets, in their cities, in their nations.

And we fight in two ways. The first is an active fight against Islamic fundamentalism – about which too many people here in this House are not talking, and are forgetting – and the other is the fight against illegal immigration: we must repatriate all illegal immigrants, because, otherwise, the security problems will get worse day by day, as the recent attacks have shown.

discussion.speaker: Regina DOHERTY
discussion.text:
A Uachtaráin, a Thaoisigh, a Aire, tá fáilte romhaibh.

Colleagues, our former Taoiseach Garret Fitzgerald said that joining Europe completed Ireland's journey to independence and history has proven him to be so right. Every generation inherits moments that define the nation and for Ireland, one of those moments was in 1973, and Ireland chose Europe. And it was a choice about the kind of country that we wanted to become: open to the world, confident and engaged and at the table instead of on the sidelines.

As we begin our eighth presidency of the Council of the European Union, the challenges that we face today are very different, but we will not be found wanting. We will give more options to build long-term financial security for the people and their families. We must find solutions for businesses struggling to grow, our young people options to buy homes and really importantly, protect our children online. And vitally, we will stand by Ukraine and the defence of Europe, even if that means having to make difficult decisions when they're not the easiest at home.

Yes, we're a small island on the western edge of Europe but, by God, we have the power and determination to help build a stronger and brighter future for...

(The President cut off the speaker)

discussion.speaker: Nina CARBERRY
discussion.text:
Madam President, Taoiseach, Ireland's EU Presidency will not be judged in this debating Chamber. It will not be judged in negotiating rooms in Brussels, Strasbourg or Dublin, nor will it happen in weeks or months after it comes to an end. But it will happen around kitchen tables. It will happen at farmyard gates and in school classrooms.

In the decades ahead, for me, there are two fences we must clear. First, farming – Europe needs a ring‑fenced common agricultural policy. It needs young farmers to see a future. It needs a pathway for retiring farmers. And it needs less red tape. Second, our children – childhood can no longer be outsourced to big tech. We need to see a ban on addictive algorithms. We need real age verification on social media. And we must pursue those who allow abusers and predators to hide behind an anonymity.

This presidency will not be judged by promises made. It will be judged by promises delivered. And we in this Parliament stand ready to work with you to achieve this.

discussion.speaker: Romana JERKOVIĆ
discussion.text:
Madam President, I welcome the Irish Presidency's commitment to strengthening Europe's health systems. Health is not a privilege, but a fundamental right, and it must remain at the heart of the European project. Innovation in life sciences, biotechnology and digital health offers enormous opportunities.

But innovation must go hand in hand with fairness. Every patient, regardless of where they live or their income, must have access to affordable medicines, high quality care and the benefits of new technologies. A resilient Europe depends on resilient public health systems supported by a well-trained and valued health workforce.

We stand ready to work with the Irish Presidency to build a health union that delivers for everyone – one that combines innovation with solidarity, competitiveness with social justice and economic growth with better health for all.

discussion.speaker: Sebastian TYNKKYNEN
discussion.text:
Arvoisa puhemies, EU-kuplassa eletään aivan toisessa todellisuudessa kuin missä tavalliset eurooppalaiset elävät. Irlanti on uusi EU-puheenjohtaja, ja tämän puheenjohtajakauden toimintaohjelma on tästä todellisuusharhasta täydellinen esimerkki.

Kun eurooppalaiset pyytävät päättäjiltä yksinkertaisia asioita, kuten turvallisuutta, kohtuuhintaista energiaa ja asumista sekä suojattuja ulkorajoja, mitä he saavat? Arvojulistuksia, LGBTIQ-ohjelmia sekä antirasismistrategioita. Tässä toimintaohjelmassa käytetään sivukaupalla tilaa siihen, mitä ihmisten pitäisi ajatella ja mitä arvoja omaksua. Nämäkö asiat valvottavat eurooppalaisia öisin? No, eivät toden totta valvota. Lakatkaa siis jo tuputtamasta näitä ideologisia ohjelmianne ja alkakaa huolehtia siitä, josta teidät on valittu pitämään huolta: siitä, että kansalaisilla on turvallinen Eurooppa, jossa leivän päälle saa muutakin kuin pelkän ylähuulen.

translation.englishText:
Dear President, in the EU bubble we live in a completely different reality than the one in which ordinary Europeans live. Ireland is the new EU presidency, and the action program for this presidency is a perfect example of this reality bias.

When Europeans ask policymakers for simple things like security, affordable energy and housing, and secure external borders, what do they get? Declarations of values, LGBTIQ programs and anti-racism strategies. In this action program, space is used in the side shop for what people should think and what values ​​to adopt. Are these things keeping Europeans up at night? Well, they don't really control it. So stop pushing these ideological programs of yours already and start taking care of what you were elected to take care of: that the citizens have a safe Europe, where you get more than just an upper lip.

discussion.speaker: Ciaran MULLOOLY
discussion.text:
Madam President, Taoiseach, one of your priorities for Ireland's Presidency is to strengthen Europe's competitiveness while protecting balanced regional development.

As you begin today to steer the negotiations on the new long-term EU budget, will you commit that Ireland will not support a deal which sidelines cohesion and rural development funds in favour of narrowly defined competitiveness spending? And can you spell out one concrete safeguard you will defend to protect our peripheral and island regions like the Midlands–North-West of Ireland?

Your shared values – we will test them in the coming months, Taoiseach. We look for human dignity when it comes to housing in particular. You know the focus. You know the crisis upon us, with 15 000 people homeless in Ireland and 5 000 children. You know we need to work harder on this.

And if there is to be a right to stay at issue in the regions of Ireland, then we need a common agricultural policy which gives all of our farmers a livelihood going forward – the small farmers and the large ones. That must be your legacy, Taoiseach, from this presidency.

discussion.speaker: Reinier VAN LANSCHOT
discussion.text:
A Uachtaráin, a Thaoisigh, is maith an scáthán súil carad.

'A friend's eye is a good mirror'. My eyes see a country a little too fond of selling aluminium to Russia and tax benefits to American tech. But I also see a country committed to peace, the best live music in Europe and a beacon of democracy. Pioneering citizen assemblies and referendums that were thoughtful and representative, instead of blunt populist tools. As pioneers of democracy, we urge you to use your presidency to fight for democracy. That means getting rid of the veto. We can act decisively and democratically, or we can have the veto. We cannot have both. If you allow me to butcher Gaelic one more time:

Am agus foighne a thógann seilide go Corcaigh.

'Time and grit and patience brings a snail to Cork'. Taoiseach, we've waited long enough. Let's get rid of the veto and bring this snail to Cork.

discussion.speaker: Maroš Šefčovič
discussion.text:
Madam President, honourable Members, I would like to thank all of you for your interventions and indeed very rich debate. The Irish Presidency has set out a clear and timely agenda, and today's discussion confirms a broad alignment on the key priorities – be it on our values, cybercrime and housing, highlighted in the interventions by Ms García Pérez and Mr Weber, or the importance of competitiveness, simplification, boosting position of European Union on the global economic stage or tackling heatwaves and fires, advocated by Ms Hayer and Ms Reintke.

Many Members of the European Parliament, Mr Mureşan, Ms Szydło, Ms Gál, Mr Flanagan, reflected in their statements the importance and complexity of the negotiations over the next multiannual financial framework. To get this done, it requires huge skills, focus and persistency, and the Irish Presidency demonstrated the ability to deliver many times in the past. I am sure, Taoiseach, that you will do it again.

To conclude, I would like to highlight that the Commission remains fully committed to work hand in hand with the presidency, the European Parliament and the Member States to deliver tangible results, because we are entering indeed a decisive phase for Europe's future. It would require true European team spirit, inter-institutional coordination and strong resolve, and I am convinced that we will all rise to the challenge as Europeans and make the European Union in the next six months under the Irish Presidency stronger and with unity.

discussion.speaker: Micheál Martin
discussion.text:
Madam President and group leaders, I want to thank everybody who contributed to the debate. I think it illustrated the rich diversity of opinion and views within this Parliament. I have taken careful note of every individual contribution. So forgive me if I perhaps just respond thematically in relation to a number of issues that were raised.

I want to thank Commissioner Šefčovič for his contribution and just to say, in the context of that contribution, that it is our belief that the Commission is taking the strategically correct decision to expand trade deals between the European Union and other countries. To counteract the increasing protectionism of others, it is important that strategically, we seek to conclude deals as effectively as we can, protecting workers' rights along that process and the essential values that underpin our economy. Our experience has been that free trade deals and trade deals benefit workers and create more jobs. That has been our experience. It can be Europe's experience into the future.

In terms of a key theme that has emerged, protecting children is uppermost in the Irish Presidency, and I thank MEP Weber for your remarks in that respect and Valérie and others spoke about the importance of the regulation and the legislation. We are looking forward to the expert panel review from the Commission. It is extremely important that we do everything we possibly can to protect our children from social media and online, and we must devise the best mechanisms to do that.

In terms of competitiveness and enterprise, Commissioner McGrath is responsible for the EU Inc. programme and idea. He comes from a country which values social partnership. We've had strong relationships with our trade union movement for decades, and we will continue to work in partnership with them. We understand the balance that has to be struck between facilitating enterprise and new ideas, but also protecting the rights of workers. But neither are mutually exclusive.

We were at the Tyndall National Institute in Cork last week with the President of the Commission and the other Commissioners, and we saw there how research and development and ideas around semiconductors and photonics lead to this formation of small companies, which provides jobs for workers, which expands and grows. The competitiveness agenda is about facilitating that dynamic and we must do it more. We have to do it faster. And it is about jobs and it is about workers.

But those small companies need to be European from day one. We cannot have national barriers against those small companies that will expand and grow and create new jobs. The savings and investments union is about underpinning that growth by providing the necessary capital to enable growth at scale, because the one weakness that researchers and people are saying to us in Europe is the absence of that capital markets union within Europe and the absence of scale. Many of our companies pivot to the US and elsewhere for that venture capital.

Could I say also that in terms of the social issue – and many spoke about housing in Ireland – housing is the number one social issue. The bulk of spending comes from the national exchequer towards housing and we are making progress, but we have to make a lot more progress so we will work hard during our presidency. We are working with the Commission to convene a special conference on housing, a summit on housing to give it that priority. We will support the Affordable Housing Act because it is something that's not just an Irish issue. As I have learned, it is across the entirety of Europe itself.

In terms of the key strengths of the European Union historically, there is no doubt – and I have listened to many Members speak about it – of the centrality and importance of food security and our farmers in particular. Our farmers have progressed over the last number of years and continue to innovate. And we must continue to support food production. I understand people's concerns in respect of cohesion, but then we have to balance that also in terms of growth, and that speaks to the budget.

That will be challenging. That is very clear from the contributions. Sometimes trying to navigate the budget negotiations is like trying to reconcile the irreconcilable in terms of different views and perspectives. But we must do it because Europe needs a budget, and we want to work with Parliament in advance and to get work done on the files, to try and prepare as much as we possibly can so that Europe is well-prepared for the next seven years. It unquestionably needs that budget.

On security, Ireland is a peacekeeping nation, always has been, militarily non-aligned, but we are not politically neutral and we understand when Russia invades Ukraine, that is a violation of the UN Charter. Europe has been consistent on that fundamental truth and we must remain so. But we must be consistent in the application of rule of law across the entirety of the Union and in all matters and in all respects. Our principled global outlook must also be consistent where all conflict and war emerges.

We will work hard with the Commission and with Parliament in particular, to advance the enhancement of capability and protection and greater resilience, particularly in terms of critical undersea infrastructure, in terms of cybersecurity and the newer hybrid threats that we are all collectively facing.

And finally, the climate issue. People have different perspectives on matters to do with climate and so on but without question, we are witnessing fairly significant events that we did not witness before. We are on the green island of Ireland and, by the way, our grass is as green as it has ever been but we have far more violent storms now, which are having greater impact. We see all the wildfires across Europe right now. Adaptation is important. We have to deal with this. There is no point in saying it's not happening. It is happening. You can have a different name for it, but Europe needs to respond in a resilient manner to these issues also.

I thank you and I look forward to working with you on the wide variety of issues that you have raised this morning. We understand what has worked for Europe, but we also understand that Europe needs to look ahead and be visionary in making sure that the generations that follow us have a Europe that they can be proud of, that they can love to live in, to work in, and to rear a family in.

discussion.speaker: Roberta METSOLA (Chair)
discussion.text:
Thank you.

The debate is closed.

Written Statements (Rule 178)

discussion.speaker: Caterina CHINNICI
discussion.text:
La situazione geopolitica globale pone l'Unione europea davanti a sfide che – per citare il motto della presidenza irlandese – possiamo affrontare solo con forza e unità.

Questo è vero per le minacce esterne, dipendenti da fattori spesso al di là del nostro controllo, e ancor più per le minacce interne, rispetto alle quali, come giustamente sottolinea il programma della presidenza irlandese, l'Unione può e deve agire con decisione.

C’è una minaccia, in particolare, che non va mai sottovalutata, perché attenta alla sicurezza dei cittadini, mina le democrazie, compromette la libertà d'impresa e si impossessa delle risorse pubbliche: è la minaccia che viene dai gruppi della criminalità organizzata, sempre più interconnessi, pericolosi e radicati nelle nostre economie.

Bene, quindi, la priorità data alla revisione dei mandati di Europol ed Eurojust, alla futura direttiva sulla criminalità organizzata, alla lotta al narcotraffico transnazionale e all'accesso ai dati a fini di contrasto, ma occorre anche garantire, nel nuovo bilancio, le risorse necessarie alle agenzie impegnate su questi fronti.

Noi, come Parlamento, faremo la nostra parte per rafforzare la risposta europea alle organizzazioni criminali: contiamo sulla presidenza irlandese per lavorare insieme, perché l'UE si dimostri davvero forte nell'unità e nel proteggere i propri cittadini.

translation.englishText:
The global geopolitical situation presents the European Union with challenges which – to quote the motto of the Irish Presidency – we can only face with strength and unity.

This is true for external threats, depending on factors often beyond our control, and even more so for internal threats, against which, as the Irish Presidency program rightly underlines, the Union can and must act decisively.

There is a threat, in particular, that should never be underestimated, because it is attentive to the safety of citizens, undermines democracies, compromises the freedom of enterprise and takes possession of public resources: it is the threat that comes from organized crime groups, which are increasingly interconnected, dangerous and rooted in our economies.

Therefore, the priority given to the review of the mandates of Europol and Eurojust, the future directive on organized crime, the fight against transnational drug trafficking and access to data for law enforcement purposes is good, but it is also necessary to guarantee, in the new budget, the necessary resources for the agencies involved on these fronts.

We, as Parliament, will do our part to strengthen the European response to criminal organisations: we count on the Irish Presidency to work together, so that the EU proves truly strong in unity and in protecting its citizens.

discussion.speaker: Loránt VINCZE
discussion.text:
Üdvözlöm az ír elnökség programját, amely a jelenlegi kihívásokra összpontosítva a versenyképesség megerősítését, Európa biztonságának növelését és a közös értékek védelmét állítja a középpontba. Különösen fontosnak tartom, hogy a program egyértelműen hivatkozik az Európai Unióról szóló szerződés 2. cikkében rögzített alapértékekre.

A Kisebbségi Intergroup elnökeként örömmel tekintek az ír elnökséggel való együttműködés folytatására. Írország sokat tett azért, hogy az ír nyelv ismét látható és élő része legyen a közéletnek. Ez azt mutatja, hogy a nyelvi sokszínűség nem csupán megőrzendő örökség, hanem olyan érték, amelyet tudatos politikákkal erősíteni és láthatóvá tenni is lehet.

Bízom benne, hogy ez a szemlélet az európai nyelvi és kulturális sokszínűség ügyében is megjelenik az elnökség munkájában. Az őshonos nemzeti és nyelvi kisebbségek támogatása nem kizárólag a jogvédelemről szól, hanem arról is, hogy az Európai Unió pozitív üzenetet közvetítsen polgárai felé: minden nyelv és kultúra hozzájárul közös európai identitásunkhoz. Ha az Unió aktívan felvállalja ezt az értéket, az különösen fontos üzenet a fiatal generációk számára, akiknek azt mutatja meg, hogy anyanyelvük és kulturális örökségük a jövő Európájában is érték és lehetőség.

Sok sikert és eredményes munkát kívánok az ír elnökségnek.

translation.englishText:
I welcome the program of the Irish Presidency, which focuses on strengthening competitiveness, increasing Europe's security and protecting common values ​​by focusing on current challenges. I consider it particularly important that the program clearly refers to the basic values ​​laid down in Article 2 of the Treaty on the European Union.

As the president of the Minority Intergroup, I look forward to continuing the cooperation with the Irish Presidency. Ireland has done a lot to make the Irish language a visible and living part of public life again. This shows that linguistic diversity is not only a heritage to be preserved, but a value that can be strengthened and made visible through conscious policies.

I trust that this approach will also be reflected in the work of the presidency in the matter of European linguistic and cultural diversity. Supporting native national and linguistic minorities is not only about legal protection, but also about the European Union conveying a positive message to its citizens: all languages ​​and cultures contribute to our common European identity. If the Union actively assumes this value, it is a particularly important message for the younger generations, to whom it shows that their mother tongue and cultural heritage are also a value and an opportunity in the Europe of the future.

I wish the Irish presidency good luck and fruitful work.
